title: Icebergs
objective: After this level you can explain why most of an iceberg is underwater.
summary: Icebergs are chunks of glacier or ice shelf, frozen fresh water from snow. Ice is only about 9% less dense than water, so about 90% of a berg floats underwater.

cards.headline: The part of an iceberg you can see is only about a tenth of it.
cards.body: About 90% hangs out of sight below the waterline. To see why, start where every iceberg starts: on land.

cards.headline: Born on land
cards.body: An iceberg isn't frozen seawater. It's a piece of a glacier or ice shelf that broke off and floated away, a break called calving. Glaciers are built from snow that piled up long enough to turn to ice, so an iceberg is frozen fresh water. Level 72's sea ice freezes in the ocean; an iceberg only ends up there. It's land ice gone to sea.

mascot.line: People mix these up all the time: sea ice froze from the sea; an iceberg came from land.

cards.headline: Greenland's iceberg factory
cards.body: Most of the icebergs that drift into North Atlantic shipping lanes come from the tidewater glaciers on Greenland's west coast, where the ice meets the sea. After breaking off, a berg takes 1 to 3 years to drift south into the lanes. Slow travelers, and not the kind you can hurry along.

cards.headline: Why ice floats low
cards.body: When water freezes, its molecules lock into an orderly lattice that holds them further apart, so ice is about 9% less dense than liquid water. That's why ice cubes float in your glass. But it's only a little lighter, so an iceberg floats low: about 90% of it sits below the waterline. The tip of the iceberg really is just the tip.

cards.headline: Icebergs: sized up
learned: An iceberg is land ice that calved into the sea
Glacier ice is frozen fresh water, from snow
Most North Atlantic bergs come from west Greenland
Ice is about 9% less dense than water
About 90% of a berg is underwater

questions.prompt: Below the waterline lies _____ of an iceberg.

options.label: about 10%
options.rationale: That is roughly the part you can see.

options.label: about half
options.rationale: Far more than half is hidden.

options.label: all
options.rationale: A little always shows above the water.

questions.explanation: Ice is only about 9% less dense than water, so about 90% of an iceberg sits below the waterline.

questions.prompt: Put an iceberg's journey in order, from first to last.
questions.explanation: Snow that piled up turns to ice and builds a glacier. A piece breaks off in calving, and the berg takes 1 to 3 years to drift south into the lanes.

questions.prompt: From Level 6, less dense water floats on denser water. What does freezing do to water that lets ice float?

options.label: Squeezes its molecules closer together
options.rationale: That would make it denser, so it would sink.

options.label: Makes it warmer than the water around it
options.rationale: Ice is colder; its lattice is what makes it lighter.

options.label: Traps extra salt inside, making it heavier
options.rationale: Salt makes water denser, and iceberg ice is fresh.

questions.explanation: Freezing locks water's molecules into an orderly lattice that holds them further apart, so ice is less dense than liquid water and floats.
